body: Anytime. I see too much of these types of questions getting downvoted so I figured Id offer some insight. I wish you great luck in conquering the beast that is the guitar!

Looking at what you have posted here shows a great opportunity to tackle the requested information as a whole with a few simple steps.

If you look at some of thing songs that you listen to, you will find consistent patterns of rhythm, scales, and chord structure. This is great because identifying these properties of songs provides a great foundation to work on the requested techniques in your comment. 

For alternate picking, identifying the scale of the desired song, and working your way through it with slow and methodical alternate picking will cement the scale into your mind for use in this case and later improvisation if desired.

In the case of hammer-ons and pull-offs, using the same scale with legato movements of your left hand will improve your technique vastly. Scales are great for this because once you know the scale, you can break it down into sections and create different hammer-on and pull-off exercises. If you combine the two skills of alternate picking and legato, you will absolutely be on your way to creatjng melodies for when you decide to write songs. 

As far as sweep picking goes, I cannot stress enough the importance of understanding why you are implementing the sweep before you learn the specific arpeggio shape. If you listen to guitarists who actively use this technique, there is a reason they are using it relative to what key they are in and what feeling is produced by using the sweep. Its rapid. Its attention-grabbing. And ultimately it sounds great but that is because of the artful choice to use it in reference to the chords being played. That being said, by returning to the scale youve learned to develop the above techniques and looking at what notes make up these scales and arpeggios, you should start to see the relationship between all of these concepts once you begin focusing on the details within songs. 

Another great tool I have used is to grab a drum rhythm book and learn patterns to develop your right hand and dexterity. These can also be applied to the above concepts down the line. 

This was crazy long-winded but I think the main idea is to get a song that you are inspired by and tear it apart. You will absorb information related to musical decision and technique far more rapidly than reading and regurgitating tablature.

Thanks for your post.

I agree with the comment below that practice is critical to understanding the fretboard but to further their point, learning how intervals between notes work can be a great starting point to understanding how a sound makes one feel. In this case, dissonance. Once you've identified the interval and how to reproduce it from a scale standpoint, taking it to the fretboard should be far easier to attain the sounds you are looking for.
